detail:
The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) describes brain stimulation therapies as treatments that activate or inhibit the brain with electricity, delivered directly through implanted electrodes, indirectly through electrodes on the scalp, or by magnetic fields applied to the head. NIMH notes these therapies are less commonly used than psychotherapy or medication, and that clinicians generally consider them when other treatments have not reduced symptoms sufficiently, including in severe or treatment-resistant depression.

NIMH divides the page between therapies authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for specific disorders and therapies still considered experimental. The authorized therapies described are electroconvulsive therapy, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, and vagus nerve stimulation. Magnetic seizure therapy and deep brain stimulation are described as experimental and available in the United States only through clinical trials or research studies. NIMH notes research is ongoing into the best use of these therapies.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about managing depression and brain stimulation therapies.
summary: NIMH describes brain stimulation therapies, including electroconvulsive therapy, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, and vagus nerve stimulation, as options clinicians consider for depression when other treatments have not worked sufficiently.
